newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian monarchists bury dead to little acclaim.
newsitem.headline: Albanian monarchists bury dead to little acclaim.

text.p: Monarchists buried a young man killed during a march that erupted into gunfire but only a modest crowd turned up for what they, and Albania's defeated ruling party, hoped would be a mass display of grief.
The body of Azim Gjonpalaj, 23, draped in a red-and-black Albanian flag topped with a royal crown, was lowered into a grave at Sharra cemetery near the capital on Saturday evening.

Mourners had borne Gjonpalaj's red coffin to the place where he was hit by gunfire on Thursday, outside the building where officials had spent all week counting the votes in Albania's general election.
Undaunted by dust and temperatures over 35 Celsius (95 Fahrenheit), they moved to Skanderbeg Square, site of most election rallies, where a sound system was being hurriedly put in place.

A long row of women, their plaited hair all but hidden beneath black mourning clothes, wept aloud as speakers blamed his death on the victorious Socialist Party and, for good measure, the Greek minority in the south of the country.

"This is not the first time that the blood of Albanians speaking up for their rights has been spilled," Abedin Mulosmani, 'court minister' of self-proclaimed King Leka, told a gathering of no more than 300.
"The flowers of freedom will take root against Communists and Greeks who call themselves Albanians."
"Down with communism!" screamed the crowd in reply.
Gjonpalaj was one of 1,500 people to die this year in violence first sparked by the demise of shady investment funds.
Leka, with two scratches over his left eye, offered condolences to the bereaved family in a brief address as well as "a message of peace and fraternity".
Thursday's protest, also attended by a few hundred monarchists, ended with gunfire scattering participants.

Led by Leka sporting military fatigues and two pistols, the marchers denounced as rigged the outcome of a referendum held last Sunday in which voters rejected a proposal to re-establish Albania's 1928-39 monarchy.

The Democratic Party, the election's big loser after five years in power in Europe's poorest country, joined forced with the monarchists to blame the Socialists for the killing. The Socialists have hinted that the outgoing party is responsible.

The Democrats "political headquarters" issued an appeal early on Saturday for its supporters to turn out to honour the memory of Gjonpalaj, a party member. But most party faithful appeared to stay away.

Genc Pollo, the party's Secretary General, said the Socialists bore responsibility for the death and were reviving a tradition of brutality as the heirs to Albania's hard-line communists, who ruled for 45 years.
The king, who returned to Albania to campaign after living virtually all his life in exile, had earlier called on the family at their home in the ramshackle suburb of Laprake.

He paid his last respects before Gjonpalaj's open coffin, tended by more than two dozen women under a make-shift canopy in the local Moslem tradition. Tucked in the dead man's fingers was a cigarette, representing a belief that people remain happy after death if given a favourite object.

Like many young Tirana residents, Gjonpalaj had left northern Albania for the relatively prosperous capital and had earned some money for a time in Greece. That had enabled him to start building the family a house of grey breeze blocks.
As the cortege moved down the rutted track leading through Laprake towards a disused and rubble-strewn air strip and hangar, men stopped working on adjacent unfinished houses.
Children ran alongside for a better view, abandoning games by some of the hundreds of thousands of concrete bunkers erected by Communist dictator Enver Hoxha to counter invaders.
"I appeal to Albania to stop all this," an unidentified family member said by the graveside. "The hand that killed him will be brought to justice."
